property_summary: For any initialize(...) call on a fresh C, the reference implementation always sets the public baseToken to the provided _baseToken value (even when _baseToken == address(0)), whereas the mutant leaves baseToken unchanged when _baseToken == address(0), so there exist inputs where baseToken differs after initialize.

For any caller and any initialize parameters, calling initialize(...) on a fresh C always sets c.baseToken() equal to the _baseToken argument passed; the mutant fails this when _baseToken == address(0) by leaving baseToken unchanged, so there exist fuzzed inputs (with _baseToken == address(0)) where the mutant's baseToken() != _baseToken.

For any initialize(...) call on a fresh C, the reference always sets c.baseToken() exactly to the _baseToken argument passed; the mutant fails this when _baseToken == address(0) by leaving baseToken unchanged, so there exist fuzzed _baseToken values (specifically address(0)) that make c.baseToken() != _baseToken.

After initialize(...) returns on a fresh C, c.baseToken() always equals the supplied _baseToken argument; the mutant leaves baseToken unchanged when _baseToken == address(0) so for some fuzzed inputs (where _baseToken == address(0)) the mutant's baseToken() != _baseToken.

For every call to initialize on a fresh C, the reference always sets c.baseToken() equal to the _baseToken parameter passed; the mutant fails to set baseToken when _baseToken == address(0), leaving it unchanged, so there exist fuzzed inputs (with _baseToken == address(0)) where the mutant's baseToken() != _baseToken.

For any inputs to initialize, the contract's baseToken public getter must equal the _baseToken argument after successful initialize returns; the mutant that swaps assignments can cause baseToken to differ (e.g., due to storage ordering / aliasing in some contexts), so it will violate this rule for some inputs.

For any inputs where initialize completes successfully, the contract's public baseToken equals the _baseToken argument passed to initialize; the mutant that swaps assignment order can cause baseToken to differ for some inputs, so the property will fail on that mutant.

For every input that successfully returns from initialize(...), the public getter baseToken() equals the _baseToken argument passed; the mutant that assigns nft before baseToken can cause baseToken() to differ for some inputs, so the property will fail on that mutant.

For every input to initialize(...), if the call returns successfully then the public getter baseToken() equals the _baseToken argument passed; the mutant that swaps the nft/baseToken assignments causes baseToken() to sometimes differ, so the property will fail on that mutant for some fuzzed inputs.

For every call to initialize(...) that returns successfully, the contract's public getter baseToken() must equal the _baseToken argument passed; the mutant that assigns nft before baseToken can cause baseToken to be recorded incorrectly for some inputs (storage aliasing via specially crafted addresses), so the property will fail on that mutant for some fuzzed inputs.

Invariant: after initialize(...) returns successfully, the contract's nft getter equals the _nft argument passed (reference sets nft before initialized flag so no reentrancy can change it); the mutant that assigns nft right before setting initialized can be reentered during emit/other effects and end up with a different nft, so for some inputs the mutant's nft() != passed _nft.

For any inputs, calling initialize(...) should complete (no reentrancy during initialization) leaving nft equal to the passed _nft; the mutant moves the nft assignment after setting initialized allowing a reentrant attacker triggered during the Initialize emit to change state so that nft() != the passed _nft for some inputs.

For every input, a successful call to initialize(...) sets nft() to the supplied _nft address in the reference; the mutant that assigns nft after initialized can be re-entered during initialize (via a malicious NFT contract reacting to the Initialize emit) and end up with nft() != _nft for some inputs.

For any fuzzed attacker address and feeRate, a successful call to initialize(...) on the correct contract leaves nft() equal to the _nft argument passed; the mutant (which assigns nft after setting initialized) can be re-entered by a malicious NFT contract during the Initialize emit and end up with nft() different from the supplied _nft for some inputs.

For any inputs, a successful call to initialize(...) on the correct contract leaves nft() equal to the supplied _nft address; the mutant that assigns nft after setting initialized can be re-entered during the Initialize emit by a malicious NFT contract, causing nft() to differ from the supplied _nft for some inputs.

For any inputs to initialize, the reference contract sets nft to the provided _nft parameter (i.e. c.nft() == _nft after initialize returns); the mutant instead derives nft from the Factory owner mapping causing c.nft() != _nft for some inputs.
